Honestly, after reading all the details, I think YTA for refusing to cancel the trip. Here’s why: You’ve been with your girlfriend for just over a year, you live together, and she was even offered the opportunity to join the trip but declined. Not only did you and your friend *rearrange plans* specifically to fit your girlfriend’s schedule—as in, making sure the trip was when she was *already committed to being out of town*—so clearly you tried to make her comfortable! However, once your third friend dropped out, you didn’t immediately tell your girlfriend, which (even if it was accidental) isn’t great given the sensitivity here.

When she did find out it would just be the two of you, her response was intense: demanded you cancel and said no way could you go. On top of that, she called it essentially a “two-night, three-day date,” claimed it betrayed her trust, and flat-out said it was like cheating. Now, you’re also facing these strict “rules” if you stay together—no initiating contact with this friend, no private hang outs, and she wants you to distance yourself from the friendship altogether. She removed you from chat apps, won’t break up, and told you to decide and just email her.

I get that your girlfriend’s rules are pretty extreme and her method of communication isn’t super healthy. I can also understand how annoying it must be after all the planning and money spent, and after already accommodating her request to move the dates. But the trip dynamic changed *drastically* from being a group hang where your girlfriend was invited, to a solo weekend away with just one friend she knows you’re close to. Not telling her right away didn’t help, and if she’s voiced insecurity about this friend before, that feels dismissive of her feelings.

If the relationship matters to you, and it is barely over a year, it’s weird to cast the girlfriend’s concerns aside when *so much* is obviously bothering her. Yes, she needs to work on trust, but you also need to reassure and respect boundaries if you see a future together. Putting the trip first (when in your girlfriend’s eyes it is now a make-or-break moment about trust and boundaries) suggests where your priorities are, and in this specific scenario, I think you’re disregarding your girlfriend’s legitimate feelings and helping escalate the conflict.

So, with ALL those facts together? Yes, I do think you’re TA for refusing to cancel. Putting a friendship or trip above a serious relationship—especially in a situation that feels so sensitive—is not the best call here.

Honestly, I don’t think you’re the asshole at all for refusing to cancel this trip. Here’s why:

You’ve been with your girlfriend for just over a year and even live together—so no one can say you’re not committed. When you initially invited your girlfriend on the trip, she *declined* to come (her choice). On top of that, at her request, you agreed to move the trip dates to when she’d be out of town, and both you and your friend rearranged your plans for her.

After a third friend dropped out (which obviously wasn’t your fault and not something you could control), everything for the trip was already booked and paid for. Yes, you maybe could have shared the update with your girlfriend sooner, but when you did, instead of having an honest conversation about boundaries or trust, she demanded you cancel and refused to “allow” the trip at all.

But what really gets me is her reaction—she straight up called the trip the equivalent of cheating, accused you of betraying her, and imposed these really strict rules: you can’t hang out with this friend at all, can’t initiate contact, and basically need to distance yourself for good. She even booted you from your chat apps and told you to email your “decision”, saying breaking up is off the table.

That level of control and jealousy goes way overboard. You did everything you could to accommodate her, and none of this reeks of betrayal. Friends are allowed to travel together, period. Relationships are built on trust, not ultimatums and isolation.

I get that insecurities can be tough, but your girlfriend’s requests aren’t reasonable. You have made a ton of concessions, and expecting you to cancel (after it’s planned and paid for) because one friend dropped out? It’s not fair to you. If she refuses to trust you and tries to dictate your friendships, that’s her issue to work out—not yours to solve by giving up your life.

So no, NTA at all. Stand firm.

Okay, so here’s my take:

You’ve been with your girlfriend (30F) for just over a year—living together—so definitely things are serious. Your skating trip with your 27F friend has been planned for a while; you and she are close from way back, and yes, *five years ago* you had some unreturned romantic feelings. But you both eventually drifted, sorted out your friendship, and have been back to being close platonically for some time. 

You, your friend, and others (including your girlfriend, who decided not to go) arranged this trip—moving the date specifically so it wouldn’t clash with your girlfriend’s plans. Both you and your friend made efforts to accommodate the request. Then a group member dropped out, but by then you’d already paid and everything was set. But as soon as it became a one-on-one trip, your girlfriend demanded you cancel and essentially wanted the final say over your plans. When you didn’t budge, things blew up between you. You see her inflexibility and distrust as a red flag, but to you and to us, your feelings for your friend are solidly platonic and you don’t expect this to change.

I have to be honest—it sounds like you’re not giving enough weight to your girlfriend’s feelings, especially considering your history with your friend. There’s a big difference between canceling fun plans because it inconveniences your partner and at least acknowledging that from her POV, this looks unusual: you both lived together, you had past feelings you felt you needed to confess, and the trip changed unexpectedly. Just because her insecurities didn’t show before doesn’t mean she isn’t feeling genuinely threatened or startled now. Dismissing it all as “controlling” doesn’t show a lot of empathy, and ignoring her distress (“let’s rethink the whole relationship!”) seems like quadrupling down. Relationships, even healthy ones, require compassion—even for stuff that feels out of nowhere. Especially for partners you say you love and live with.

You asked AITA for refusing to cancel. Honestly, *yes*. A little more perspective-taking, or being ready to reconsider plans (even after payment, *especially* after all that) would have been kinder—especially if you value your relationship with your girlfriend as highly as your trip with a platonic friend.

Okay, here’s my take: 

No, you are absolutely NTA for refusing to cancel the trip with your friend just because of your girlfriend’s sudden insecurities. You’ve been open and went above and beyond to respect her comfort: you invited her to join, moved the trip so she'd be away and not feel weird about it, and kept her in the loop the whole time. Frankly, that’s more courtesy than a lot of people extend in these kinds of situations.

Let’s review—your girlfriend knew about the history with your friend and never seemed bothered before; you had a crush five years ago, never reciprocated, got distance, then rebuilt a close, clearly platonic friendship. Both of you took pains to ensure your girlfriend was considered in the planning. Now everything’s booked, the third friend drops out, and suddenly she demands you cancel and forbids you to go? That just shouts controlling and distrustful, especially given there’s no evidence from your side that anything romantic would ever happen.

It sounds to me like you handled this as maturely as possible: you offered transparency, adjusted plans, communicated openly, and even pointed out your partner’s unreasonable demands could be a relationship problem if trust is lacking. Time to go enjoy your skating trip guilt-free. If your girlfriend can’t trust you—when you’ve given no reason not to—that’s her insecurity to work on, not yours to cater to.

So yeah. Stand your ground—you’ve done everything right!

Honestly, based on everything you’ve described, I do think YTA for refusing to cancel the skating trip with your friend, even though I get that you mean well.

Here are the facts: You and your 27F friend have been extremely close since school and university. You even had unreciprocated romantic feelings for her five years ago, which might still be on your girlfriend's mind, even though you drifted apart and now your friendship is purely platonic. Reconnecting and maintaining close friendships is wonderful. But in this specific case, I feel like your girlfriend's feelings are being overlooked.

To go over the situation: You and your friend planned a skating trip this year, just like you did and enjoyed in university. Others were invited—including your girlfriend—who chose not to go. When your girlfriend expressed discomfort about the trip, you both rearranged it to happen while your girlfriend is conveniently out of town, to help her feel more secure. Now that a third friend has backed out, it will just be you and this female friend for several days, booked and paid for already.

The complication? From your girlfriend’s perspective, it looks bad. She directly told you this situation betrays her trust, equating it with cheating and "a date". She’s now set rules that you shouldn’t initiate contact, hang out privately, or be so close. To your credit, you believe your relationship with this friend is purely platonic, and that nothing romantic will ever develop.

But in relationships, it isn’t always about what's “actually” happening—it’s also about respecting what your partner feels. In this scenario, after years of history, shifting plans, past feelings, & your friend now being your *closest friend again*, plus the intimate setting—you can see why your girlfriend feels anxious and betrayed and thinks her boundaries are fair. Even if you think she's being insecure, ignoring her very strong discomfort signals disregard for her feelings.

So yes, YTA here. By refusing to cancel—especially given ALL the history, and especially after your girlfriend made her concerns so clear—you’re prioritizing your friendship over your relationship, and dismissing your girlfriend’s deep insecurities. At the very least, this whole situation should be a big conversation with her, with full transparency and understanding. Ignoring her concerns or going ahead anyway isn’t okay.

Honestly, in this situation, I don’t think I’m the asshole for refusing to cancel the trip with my friend over my girlfriend’s insecurities. Here’s why:

My friend (27F) and I have a long-standing friendship — we’ve been close since school and even went to university together. Yes, I did have some unreciprocated romantic feelings for her five years ago, but things NEVER went anywhere, and we naturally drifted apart a bit after that. Recently, we repaired that friendship, and it’s now strictly platonic from my end (and hers too).

This skating trip isn’t some spontaneous new “date.” We did a similar trip together in university and really enjoyed it. So it’s like a tradition — we only just got the chance to plan it again this year. Not to mention, we did invite other people, including my girlfriend, but she refused to come.

To make my girlfriend feel more comfortable, we even *moved* the trip to a weekend when she would be out of town — that took considerable effort to reschedule for both my friend and me! We tried to include others, but the only other person who was supposed to join backed out last minute, so now it’s just the two of us with everything already booked and paid for.

Now, my girlfriend is saying that it’s basically a romantic getaway, calling it a “two-night, three-day date,” claiming I’m betraying her trust, and even comparing it to cheating. On top of that, she’s setting these rules telling me I’m not allowed to privately hang out with my friend, initiate contact with her, or otherwise maintain the friendship as it was.

Frankly, I’ve already gone out of my way to reassure my girlfriend: my feelings toward my friend are 100% platonic now, and I can’t see that ever changing. Canceling this trip, which we planned months in advance and have invested in (emotionally and financially), just because partners should keep zero contact or friendship with anyone they once had feelings for, seems unreasonable to me. If canceling this means bowing to excessive jealousy or a lack of trust, then where does it end?

My friendship with my friend does not threaten my romantic relationship, and I’ve shown more than enough effort to work around my girlfriend’s feelings without losing an important connection in my life. So, no, I don’t think I’m the asshole for keeping plans with my friend and not giving in to unfair ultimatums.

Honestly, after reading about this situation, I think YTA for refusing to cancel the trip. So here’s why: 

You (26F) have been with your girlfriend (30F) for over a year and even live together, so that’s a serious level of commitment. But you decided to plan a trip with a close friend (27F) with whom you *used to* have unreciprocated romantic feelings (back in the day), and now you and this friend have recently grown close again after some time apart. 

When you told your girlfriend it would be just the two of you on this trip, she was upfront about not being okay with it and even told you to cancel, setting clear boundaries about your contact and relationship with this friend. From your post, it seems she’s not *normally* insecure about your friend, which suggests maybe your rekindled closeness and this trip really did make her uncomfortable—for pretty reasonable reasons, IMO.  

When she asked you to respect her boundaries, you doubled down, refused to call it off, and even said you two should rethink the relationship because of her “control” and “lack of trust.” That would seriously hurt in any relationship! After that, your girlfriend did cut you off on social apps and went radio silent, which might seem harsh, but keep in mind she tried to set boundaries first.

At the end of the day, you have a right to your friends, but knowing the complicated history and the seriousness of your relationship, I think it was too much to ask of your girlfriend to just be fine with it. Her reaction wasn’t perfect, but I think YOU are TA for putting more value on this trip (and this friend) than on your partner’s legitimate concerns. 

To sum up: You may not agree with your girlfriend’s rules, but just dismissing her feelings as controlling rather than trying to work things out was unfair, especially since she hasn’t acted unreasonable in the past. So, yes, YTA.

Absolutely not the asshole here. Here’s how I see it:

You’ve been with your girlfriend for just over a year and already live together, and until now, she hasn’t showed any insecurities about your close (but strictly platonic) friendship with your friend from school/university. It’s wild to me that all of a sudden, as soon as you planned this trip (just the two of you), she not only demanded you cancel, but basically handed you a list of isolation rules: no contacting your friend, no hanging out with her privately, and basically wants you to completely distance yourself. That’s not healthy or reasonable, especially since you were upfront about the history: yes, you did have feelings five years ago and nothing happened. That’s well in the past, and you’ve clearly made amends as friends.

Refusing to cancel and telling your girlfriend to think about whether this relationship was working for her given her trust issues makes perfect sense. It sounds like her reaction went full-on dramatic—removing you from chat apps, refusing to break up but tossing everything in your lap with an ultimatum is just more controlling behavior.

If she didn’t have an issue before, her sudden, drastic rules suggest this is about control, not concern. You shouldn’t have to choose between your relationship and a long-time, important (now actually platonic) friendship. The fact that she tried to isolate you says a lot.

So no, you’re not the asshole for refusing to cancel the trip. Setting healthy boundaries (and sticking up for yourself) when your partner acts controlling is absolutely justified.
